debate.situation: You have received a job offer with a 25 percent pay increase, but it requires a three-hour daily commute. You are struggling to determine if the financial gain outweighs the significant loss of personal time.

minds.title: The Utilitarian
minds.concern: Maximizing net pleasure and minimizing pain through careful calculation.
minds.author: Jeremy Bentham
minds.book: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

minds.title: The Essentialist
minds.concern: Prioritizing the vital few tasks and eliminating the trivial many.
minds.author: Greg McKeown

minds.title: The Stoic
minds.concern: Maintaining internal tranquility regardless of external circumstances.
minds.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Utilitarian
debate.text: You might view this as a simple felicific calculus, where the pleasure of increased income must be weighed against the pain of fifteen hours lost to travel each week.
debate.author: Jeremy Bentham
debate.book: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
debate.basis: Basis: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

debate.speaker: The Essentialist
debate.text: I would argue that you are facing a classic trade-off, where choosing the higher pay means sacrificing your most precious resource, which is time, and you should consider if the gain is truly essential.
debate.author: Greg McKeown

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: Perhaps you fear that the commute will disturb your peace, but remember that the mind is its own place, and you might find tranquility even in a long journey if you focus on what is within your control.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Utilitarian
debate.text: The Essentialist assumes that time is always the primary metric, but if the extra money allows you to purchase services that save you more time at home, the net pleasure might actually increase.
debate.author: Jeremy Bentham
debate.book: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
debate.basis: Basis: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

debate.speaker: The Essentialist
debate.text: The Utilitarian claims that money can buy back time, but this ignores the reality that some experiences, like rest or presence with family, cannot be outsourced or purchased with a salary increase.
debate.author: Greg McKeown

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: The Essentialist suggests that rest is a requirement for a good life, but you might find that your character is forged precisely by enduring the external conditions you cannot change.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Utilitarian
debate.text: I drop my claim that this is a simple sum of pleasure versus pain, as the Essentialist correctly points out that some losses, like presence with family, are qualitative and defy easy arithmetic.
debate.author: Jeremy Bentham
debate.book: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
debate.basis: Basis: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

debate.speaker: The Essentialist
debate.text: To test your limits, try a one-week experiment where you wake up and spend three hours in transit before starting your current day to see if your energy levels remain sustainable.
debate.author: Greg McKeown

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: Testing this for one week respects your constraint of time, but it carries the cost of potential burnout before you even begin the new role, which might cloud your judgment about your own resilience.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.clearer: The debate clarifies that the decision is not just about money versus time, but about whether the commute represents a manageable challenge or a fundamental degradation of your quality of life. The main disagreement remains whether your internal state can adapt to the commute or if the time loss is an objective, non-negotiable cost.
debate.dependsOn: If your current financial situation is precarious, the 25 percent increase may be a necessity that outweighs the time cost. If you are financially stable, the decision depends on whether you value the extra money more than the three hours of daily autonomy. To decide, calculate exactly how much of that 25 percent increase will be spent on commuting costs, as this will reveal the true net gain.
